corpus.title: ‘Hit them hard’: Does Trump have another ‘new’ Iran strategy, can it work?
corpus.signal_text:
‘Hit them hard’: Does Trump have another ‘new’ Iran strategy, can it work?
Trump signals harsher response as US-Iran hostilities escalate, raising fears of prolonged conflict in the Gulf region.
Following the first strikes in the US-Iran war for a month, this week, United States President Donald Trump appeared to signal a new phase in the war, which marked its first six months on Friday last week.
“We’re going to hit them hard … there will be a response,” Trump told reporters on Monday, shortly after Iran launched missile attacks on US military sites in Jordan in response to its strikes on Iran’s Larak Island the previous night.

US news outlet Axios reported Washington may be switching to a new “no war, no peace” strategy in the conflict in which it aims to hit Iran periodically without engaging in a sustained conflict.
So, what exactly is Trump’s strategy now, and can the US military sustain it as the war enters its seventh month?
What happened on Monday?
The US struck military targets on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, close to Iran’s strategic port of Bandar Abbas. Washington said its forces hit two Iranian rocket launchers which it claimed the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was preparing to use to scatter sea mines into the strait.
Iranian media reported three people were killed. Iran subsequently launched missiles at two airbases hosting US military personnel and assets in Jordan. Jordan said it intercepted eight missiles. In turn, Trump pledged to respond, saying: “We’re going to hit them hard.”
Speaking at a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said his forces would cease fire if the US did the same, and if it fulfilled its commitments under an interim deal signed in June to end the war, lift sanctions and open the Strait of Hormuz. That deal has since expired, however, and largely fell apart because of disagreements arising from its vague wording.
Monday’s exchange of fire marked the first direct attacks between the two sides in more than a month and raised fears that the conflict could return to a more intense military phase.

U.S.-Iran Fighting Reignites
A U.S. attack on Larak Island paves the way for renewed heavy warfare.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the United States’ attack on Iran’s Larak Island, a rising flood death toll in Nepal, and Greece’s multibillion-dollar defense deal with Israel.
Targeting the Islands
U.S. and Iranian forces exchanged fire on Sunday and Monday for the first time since late July, once against casting doubt on the White House’s repeated claims that the monthslong conflict is nearing its end.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the United States’ attack on Iran’s Larak Island, a rising flood death toll in Nepal, and Greece’s multibillion-dollar defense deal with Israel.
Targeting the Islands
U.S. and Iranian forces exchanged fire on Sunday and Monday for the first time since late July, once against casting doubt on the White House’s repeated claims that the monthslong conflict is nearing its end.
According to a U.S. official, the United States struck Iran’s critical Larak Island on Sunday, damaging two rocket launchers. The official said that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was “observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into [the] Strait of Hormuz.” Local authorities claimed that the U.S. attack killed at least two people and wounded several others.
Hitting Larak, the closest island along the Strait of Hormuz, carries strategic significance, as the IRGC has used it to host military activity, monitor global shipping, and exert influence over the thoroughfare. The United States has previously targeted other Iranian islands—such as Qeshm, Kharg, and Greater Tunb—in a bid to undermine Iran’s maritime authority and deny the regime access to valuable military and economic hubs.
Also on Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump posted an artificial intelligence-generated video on social media depicting a fictional incident in which U.S. forces attack Kharg Island. Vice President J.D. Vance said on Monday that the video was an effort by Trump to send a message to Tehran to stop shooting at commercial shipping “or there are going to be some consequences.”
In response to the Larak strike, Iranian forces launched ballistic missiles at two U.S. military bases in Jordan on Sunday. Tehran will “not hesitate to exercise the inherent right of legitimate defense and will respond decisively to any military aggression,” the Iranian Foreign Ministry said on Monday.
